to separate the day from the night
phrases.literal: 'to-separate between the-day and-between the-night'; 'between...and between' is rendered 'from'

grammar: יְהִי is singular before the plural מְאֹרֹת; Ibn Ezra notes that the verb 'to be' often does not agree in number or gender (cf. Deut 22:23 כִּי יִהְיֶה נַעֲרָה).
לְהַבְדִּיל is an infinitive of purpose; the pashta on מְאֹרֹת and the zaqef on הַשָּׁמַיִם set off 'lights in the expanse' from the purpose clause.
The etnaḥta on הַלָּיְלָה divides the verse: purpose of separation, then the further functions after it.
וְהָיוּ is a weqatal continuing the jussive, so it is also a wish-command: 'and let them be'.
The four ל-phrases (signs, appointed times, days, years) are a list; whether the ל of לְאֹתֹת governs all four is debated, and Ibn Ezra rejects the view that the ל is superfluous.
segments.note: מְאֹרֹת is written without vav; Rashi hears מְאֵרָה 'curse' in it, which is homiletic and not adopted. 'Appointed times' follows Rashi's reading of the festivals; Ibn Ezra glosses 'signs and times' as portents and hours, kept in the notes.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the lights were created on the first day and on the fourth day God commanded them to be hung in the expanse; everything was created on day one and fixed on its own day. This is about order of creation, not the sense of the words.
Rashi: מְאֹרֹת is written defectively (מארת), because the fourth day is a day of curse (מְאֵרָה), when diphtheria strikes children. A homiletic reading, not adopted in the English.

Rashi: 'to separate between day and night' is after the first light was stored away; during the seven days of creation the first light and darkness served day and night together. Bears on the cosmic history, not the English.
Rashi: when the luminaries are eclipsed it is a bad omen for the world (Jer 10:2). 'Signs' is the English rendering.
Rashi: 'appointed times' is said for the future, when Israel will be commanded concerning the festivals, which are counted by the birth of the moon. The English keeps 'appointed times' for מוֹעֲדִים.
Rashi: the work of the sun is half a day and that of the moon is half, together a whole day. 'Days' is kept.
Rashi: at the end of 365 days the lights complete their course through the twelve constellations, which is a year, and begin again. 'Years' is kept.

Ibn Ezra: the word יְהִי means 'will be'; because it is used so often it serves singular and plural and also feminine, as in 'if there be a virgin girl' (Deut 22:23). The English 'let there be lights' follows.

Ibn Ezra: 'for signs, moments and seasons', that is, hours; the signs may also mean portents of eclipse of moon and sun (Jer 10:2). He rejects the view that the ל of לְאֹתֹת is superfluous. The English keeps 'signs'; the 'hours' reading is recorded here.

Ibn Ezra: a great Spanish sage held that the expanse is divided into eight parts; Ibn Ezra rejects this, and holds that the sun, moon and stars are lights in the expanse because they are seen there. The English 'in the expanse of the sky' follows.

apparatus: Onkelos renders 'lights' by נְהוֹרִין and 'appointed times' by זִמְנִין, 'and to count by them days and years'.
Radak: בְּרָקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם is the air; Ramban reads the lights as formed from the heavens' substance.

phrases.english: in the expanse of the sky
to give light on the earth

grammar: וְהָיוּ is weqatal: the command continues, with a new purpose added to the first.
לְהָאִיר is Hiphil: 'to cause light', as against the Qal 'be light'.
The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ closes the command; וַיְהִי־כֵן is a separate short clause after it.
segments.note: The verse repeats 'lights in the expanse'; Rashi and Radak take it as adding a function: that they give light to the earth, in addition to marking time.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'they shall serve this too, to give light to the world'. The English keeps the added purpose 'to give light on the earth'.
Ramban: the addition is that their light reaches the earth, since they could have been seen in the sky without lighting the earth.
Radak: 'and let them also be lights'; the lights existed before, but on day four they were hung in the expanse to give light to those who see.

apparatus: Onkelos: וִיהוֹן לִנְהוֹרִין בִּרְקִיעָא דִּשְׁמַיָּא לְאַנְהָרָא עַל אַרְעָא וַהֲוָה כֵן.

'[mark] the-luminary the-great'; the positive adjective is read as comparative

grammar: אֵת marks each definite direct object; here it is repeated for the two lights and for the stars.
הַגָּדוֹל and הַקָּטֹן are positive adjectives used where English says 'greater' and 'lesser'.
לְמֶמְשֶׁלֶת is the construct of מֶמְשָׁלָה: 'for the dominion of the day'.
The etnaḥta on הַגְּדֹלִים divides the verse; the stars are added in a short last clause under the silluq.
וְאֵת הַכּוֹכָבִים has no verb of its own: it depends on וַיַּעַשׂ and is added almost as an afterthought.
segments.note: הַמְּאֹרֹת הַגְּדֹלִים is 'great' relative to the stars, as Ibn Ezra and Radak say (they are not great in body but in light); the grammatical form is a masculine plural adjective with a feminine plural noun.

commentary.summary: Rashi: they were created equal, and the moon was made smaller because she accused, saying two kings cannot use one crown. A homily; the English says 'two great lights' and 'greater' and 'lesser' without it.
Rashi: because He made the moon smaller He multiplied her hosts, to appease her. A homiletic comment on the stars.
Ibn Ezra: the two are called great against the stars, as the three eldest sons of Jesse are called the great ones against the others. The English 'great' follows.
Ibn Ezra: the rule of the day is the sun's rule by day and not by night; 'the great' is of their light, not their bodies, and the moon's light is doubled because she is near the earth.
Ramban: the lights were not made of the body of the expanse but are bodies set in it.
Radak: 'great' here is of their light, not body, since the stars are greater than the moon in body.

apparatus: Onkelos: וְיָת נְהוֹרָא רַבָּא לְמִשְׁלַט בִּימָמָא; the verbs and nouns are the same as the Hebrew.

grammar: אֹתָם is the object marker with a pronoun suffix: 'them'; it stands before the subject אֱלֹהִים.
נָתַן here is 'set, place', not 'give'; Ibn Ezra cites Gen 9:13.
The tevir on אֹתָם and the etnaḥta on הַשָּׁמָיִם mark the two parts of the verse.
segments.note: נָתַן is 'put, set' (Qal 2). Radak takes וַיִּתֵּן as the placing of the lights in the expanse, which they had not been in until day four.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: do not wonder at וַיִּתֵּן, since it is written 'I have set my bow in the cloud' (Gen 9:13). The English 'set' follows.
Radak: וַיִּתֵּן is said after וַיַּעַשׂ because it means He placed them in the expanse, where they had not been before the fourth day (text cut in the pack).
Radak: with 'to give light' joined to 'and to rule', 'to give light' refers to their light and 'to rule' to their effect.

apparatus: The pack text of radak:1:17:1 is cut; summary taken from the part given.

segments.literal: and-to-rule in-the-day and-in-the-night and-to-separate between the-light and-between the-darkness and-saw God that good

wayyiqtol

phrases.english: and to rule over the day and the night
and to separate the light from the darkness

phrases.literal: 'that good'; no verb in Hebrew, 'it was' is supplied

grammar: The two infinitives, 'to rule' and 'to separate', continue the purpose of verse 17.
בַּיּוֹם has the article fused into the preposition בַּ.
וּלְהַבְדִּיל takes the vocalization of an unstressed ל after וּ with a secondary stress mark (ֽ).
הָאוֹר and הַחֹשֶׁךְ are the 'light' and 'darkness' of day one: whether these refer to day and night, or to light and dark as such, is discussed by the commentators.
The etnaḥta on הַחֹשֶׁךְ divides the verse before the evaluation, 'God saw that it was good'.
segments.note: The light/darkness of the separation echoes verses 4 and 5; Ramban takes אוֹר and חֹשֶׁךְ as the day and the night; Ibn Ezra takes them as the daytime light of the sun and the nighttime light of the moon. The English keeps the plain 'the light from the darkness'.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: the day of the Torah runs from sunrise to sunset, and the night from the appearance of the stars; with the light of the sun by day and the moon by night, the lights separate the light from the darkness. The English keeps 'to rule over the day and the night' and 'to separate the light from the darkness'.

Ramban: 'rule' covers the sign-giving of verse 14, since the lights rule over changes on earth; sun by day causes growth, moon by night fertility. A further reading is that rule is the power of emanation. These readings of 'rule' are recorded here, not put in the English.
Ramban disagrees with Ibn Ezra: 'light' and 'darkness' here are the names of day and night (v. 5); the great light rules in the day and the small in the night.
Radak: from sunrise it is light, which is the day, and from the appearance of the stars it is darkness, called thus because it is dark relative to the light of day.

apparatus: Variant: WLC reads וּלֲהַבְדִּיל for MAM וּלְהַבְדִּיל in 1:18.4 (vowel only).

grammar: The formula is the same as for the previous days: evening first, then morning.
יוֹם רְבִיעִי is indefinite, 'a fourth day', whereas the sixth day alone has the article.
A paragraph mark (פ) follows the verse, ending the section.
segments.note: Day, evening and morning are the same as in verses 5, 8 and 13; the ordinal is without the article.

commentary.summary: Targum Onkelos: וַהֲוָה רְמַשׁ וַהֲוָה צְפַר יוֹם רְבִיעָאִי; it matches the Hebrew, evening and morning, a fourth day.
